# Guardrails & Executable Governance

**Table of Contents**

- [1. Strategic Intent: Constraint-Based Design](#1-strategic-intent-constraint-based-design)
- [2. The Salesforce "Governor" Rosetta Stone](#2-the-salesforce-governor-rosetta-stone)
- [3. AWS FinOps & Serverless Guardrails (Phase 8)](#3-aws-finops--serverless-guardrails-phase-8)
- [4. Quality Gates & DevOps Discipline](#4-quality-gates--devops-discipline)
- [5. Request Lifecycle & Governance Gates](#5-request-lifecycle--governance-gates)
- [6. The Three-Gate Approval Process](#6-the-three-gate-approval-process)
- [7. Business Impact of Executable Governance](#7-business-impact-of-executable-governance)

---

Project: Salesforce Platform Architect Portfolio

Owner: Ryan Bumstead

Version: 1.0

Status: live since October 2026, with the static front end live since 2026-11-09

This document outlines the governance framework and constraint-based design principles that let the portfolio run on a zero budget while it keeps to enterprise quality, security and performance habits. Where a performance target is not met, the measured number is given.

## 1. Strategic Intent: Constraint-Based Design

This portfolio is built on a "Zero-Dollar Budget" requirement. That is not a limitation. It is an architectural challenge. We demonstrate **Constraint-Based Design** by building a resilient, observable system that runs within the strict limits of a Salesforce Developer Edition (free tier). The AWS Always-Free design in section 3 is Designed for a later phase: the repository holds no AWS code.

> [!TIP]
> **Why Constraint-Based Design Matters**: Many architects treat free tiers as temporary scaffolding. This portfolio shows a production system built within zero-budget constraints, a skill that translates directly to cost optimization in enterprise environments where every dollar of cloud spend requires justification.

## 2. The Salesforce "Governor" Rosetta Stone

**What are Governor Limits?** Salesforce runs on shared infrastructure (multitenant), so it enforces strict limits per transaction to prevent one customer from monopolizing resources. Think of it like apartment building rules: no playing loud music after 10pm so everyone can sleep. These "governors" force developers to write efficient code.

We treat these limits as a blueprint for building high-performance systems.

| Salesforce Constraint                | What It Means                                                                                                                                    | Enterprise Pattern Applied               | Portfolio Implementation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **100 SOQL Queries per transaction** | SOQL (Salesforce Object Query Language) is like SQL for databases. You get 100 database queries per page load. Exceed this and your app crashes. | **Bulkification** (batch processing)     | A `SAPI*` list read runs a fixed number of queries whatever the record count: one page query and one `COUNT()` query through `QueryDefinitions` (for example `SAPIContact.cls` lines 36 and 43), plus the rate limit read in `RateWindowLimiter`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **10 second CPU timeout**            | Your code gets 10 seconds of processing time. After that, Salesforce kills it to protect other customers.                                        | **Async Strategy** (offload work)        | No heavy work runs in Apex while a visitor waits. The resume PDF is drawn in the browser with jsPDF ([ADR-023](../adr/023-client-side-pdf-generation-jspdf-for-mvp.md)), and GitHub and Jira are read by scheduled Queueable jobs, so a page view never makes a callout. Moving PDF generation to AWS Lambda is a Phase 8 design and is Designed only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **6MB Heap Size**                    | Your code can only use 6MB of memory per transaction. For context, a single high-res image is ~5MB.                                              | **Lazy Loading** (load only when needed) | The D3.js graph engine (`D3_Library`, 81,482 bytes, with pan, zoom and drag) loads only when a visitor opens a graph view, and never on a phone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Guest User Security**              | Anonymous visitors have restricted permissions by default. They can't see sensitive data without explicit grants.                                | **Zero Trust** (deny by default)         | `Portfolio_Guest` grants read on six portfolio objects, create and read on `Testimonial__c`, and no permission on Account, Contact or any other standard object apart from read on `UserExternalCredential`. The few records a page needs beyond that, such as my Contact for the resume header, are read by Apex in system mode through `without sharing` selectors that select a fixed list of public fields and never an email, phone or address (`ResumeController.ResumeSelector`, `PortfolioGroundingService.Selector`). The guest reaches that data only through the shape the controller returns. |
| **Real-time Telemetry**              | Salesforce provides APIs to check how close you are to hitting limits.                                                                           | **Glass Box Telemetry** (show your work) | Governor limits (SOQL count, heap usage, CPU time) displayed in site footer so visitors can see the system is healthy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Key Insight:** These aren't arbitrary restrictions. They force the same discipline required in any high-scale system (database query optimization, memory management, async processing).

## 3. AWS FinOps & Serverless Guardrails (Phase 8)

| Phase       | Status       | Rationale                                                                  |
| :---------- | :----------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Phase 8** | **Designed** | Designed to show how the site would scale out, and left out of the launch. |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Everything about AWS in this section is Designed, and none of it is built.** The repository holds no AWS code, and no Lambda function, storage bucket or CloudWatch log group serves the portfolio. The Lambda, VPC and CloudWatch parts below are the Phase 8 design. The Gemini quota part describes what runs today.

> [!NOTE]
> **Architectural Reference:** For the detailed system diagrams and component specifications of the Phase 8 architecture, please refer to the **[Systems Architecture Specification (SAS)](./03-SAS.md#11-architectural-north-star)**.

**What is FinOps?** Financial Operations (FinOps) is the practice of making cloud costs visible and controllable. AWS charges for everything (compute time, network traffic, log storage), so architectural decisions directly impact the monthly bill.

To keep the design at $0.00 a month, the architecture avoids common "cost traps":

### Lambda Function URLs vs API Gateway

**The Problem:** AWS Lambda (serverless functions) needs a way for the internet to reach it. The "official" way is API Gateway, which is billed per request once its 12 month free tier ends.

**Our Solution:** Lambda Function URLs (direct HTTP access) are free forever and sufficient for this use case. We sacrifice advanced features (request throttling, API keys) to stay within the free tier.

**Trade-off:** In production, we'd use API Gateway for better security controls. For a portfolio, Function URLs prove we understand cost architecture.

---

### The "No-VPC" Rule

**The Problem:** A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is AWS's isolated network. Running Lambda inside a VPC is considered "best practice" for security, but it requires a NAT Gateway to reach the internet. A NAT Gateway is billed by the hour just to exist, even with zero traffic.

**Our Solution:** Run Lambda functions outside a VPC. They can still call public APIs (Salesforce, GitHub) securely via HTTPS without the NAT Gateway tax.

**Trade-off:** Can't access private databases (RDS, private subnets). For this portfolio, all data lives in Salesforce, so we don't need VPC isolation.

---

### Gemini API Quota Management

**The Problem:** The Gemini API key's free tier allowed Gemini 2.5 Flash 5 requests per minute and 20 requests per day when it was read on 2026-10-20 (a recorded reading, not a live one). Flash reasons before it answers and spends most of its tokens on that, so only a few cover letters a minute fit and few a day. Past the limit, Google answers HTTP 429.

**Our Solution:** No quota counter is stored and no Platform Cache is used (the org has no partition). The bounds are:

- The `papi-ai` rate tier of `RateWindowLimiter`: 10 requests a minute on `POST /papi/ai/generate`, and a separate 10 a minute for the site's cover letter page, shared by every visitor (`papi-ai:site-cover-letter`).
- When Google refuses or fails, the cover letter falls back to the Local Template, so the visitor still gets a letter (`ContentGenerationController.dispatch`).
- The footer shows "AI requests today", the sum of today's `papi-ai` counts in `API_Rate_Window__c`. It counts requests, not Gemini calls, and a Local fallback counts too, so it is never labelled as a Gemini quota (my decision, 2026-10-21).

---

### CloudWatch Logs Retention

**The Problem:** AWS charges for log storage beyond its free allowance. Lambda functions generate logs every time they run.

**Our Solution:** Set retention to 1 day (minimum allowed). Production environments would use 30-90 days for incident investigation, but this portfolio prioritizes cost over long-term debugging.

## 4. Quality Gates & DevOps Discipline

**What are Quality Gates?** Automated checks that block bad code from reaching production. Think of them as airport security scanners for software.

We enforce "Green Builds" through automated gatekeeping in our GitHub Actions pipelines:

### Test Coverage (90% Required)

**What it measures:** Percentage of code executed by automated tests.  
**Our standard:** a pull request fails when any Apex test fails or when org wide coverage is under 90%. `pr.yml` deploys the branch to a fresh scratch org, runs every local test with coverage, and passes the result to `scripts/coverage-gate.js --min 90` (`pr.yml`, "Deploy & Test (Scratch Mode - FULL)"). The same script runs locally with `npm run sf:coverage -- --target-org <alias>` and as a step of `npm run pre-launch-check`. The threshold is also listed in the **[Program Charter: Success Criteria](./02-Program-Charter.md#22-success-criteria-definition-of-done)**.  
**Why it matters:** Untested code fails in production. High coverage catches bugs before customers see them.

---

### Static Analysis (Salesforce Code Analyzer)

**What it does:** Scans code for common mistakes (unused variables, SOQL injection risks, performance anti-patterns) with PMD and ESLint rules.  
**Our rule:** `npm run scan` runs `sf code-analyzer` over `packages` with `--severity-threshold 2`, so any violation at severity 1 (Critical) or 2 (High) fails the run. The `quality-check` job of `pr.yml` runs it on every pull request.

---

### LCP Target (2.5 seconds)

**What is LCP?** Largest Contentful Paint: the time until the main content appears on screen. Google uses this for search ranking.  
**Our target:** 2.5 seconds (Google's "good" threshold, which applies to the 75th percentile of real visits). The production Lighthouse audit of 2026-11-12 measured mobile LCP medians of 2.2 to 2.9 s on the six main routes. That is lab data, three runs a route, and not a Core Web Vitals result. Two route medians are under 2.5 s, three are within 0.03 s above it, and the home page is the slowest at 2.92 s ([Technical Guide §2.11](./04-Technical-Guide.md#211-mobile-performance) names the tool, the emulation and the environment). The Experience Cloud site measured 7.5 to 10.6 s, and those figures stay in the Technical Guide as history.  
**How we enforce:** LCP and performance only warn. The static site workflow (`site.yml`) runs a six route, three run Lighthouse audit on every pull request and every merge to `main`, and reports the medians in the job summary. A pull request audits a local copy of the build on the runner, and a merge audits `https://ryanbumstead.com` after the deploy. The one failing assertion is accessibility, which must read 100 on every route of a pull request. Lighthouse also runs on demand (`performance.yml`, started by hand with a target URL, which runs `npm run test:lighthouse`).  
**Why it matters:** Slow sites lose users, and LCP is one of the signals Google uses for search ranking.

---

### Delta Deployment Strategy

**What it does:** Instead of deploying every metadata file on every change, the production deploy sends only what changed since the last successful production deploy. GlassOps plans that change from the git tag `glassops/deployed/prod`, validates it check only, gates it with a signed PERMIT after my approval, deploys it and verifies production, and the tag moves only after a deploy.  
**Strategic Value:** A small change deploys as a small package, so a release is quicker and touches less of the org. No timing has been measured, so none is claimed.  
**Implementation:** For the technical configuration of `sfdx-git-delta` in the pipeline, see **[Maintenance Guide: Delta Deployment](./05-Maintenance-Guide.md#33-pipeline-strategy-delta-deployment)**.

---

### Scratch Org Validation

**What is a Scratch Org?** A temporary, isolated Salesforce environment created from source control. Think "Docker container for Salesforce."  
**Our process:** Every pull request that touches `packages/**` creates a one day scratch org, deploys the whole of `packages` to it, runs every local test through the coverage gate above, then GlassOps validates the PR's delta check only against production with `RunRelevantTests`, the tests Salesforce picks from the delta ("Validate Delta Against Production (GlassOps, Check Only)"), so a component or relevant test that fails only in production stops the PR before the merge, and deletes the org. When the scratch org cannot be created, the job falls back to that delta dry run against production on its own (`pr.yml`, "Deploy & Test (Fallback Mode - DELTA)").  
**Why it matters:** Catches "works on my machine" issues. If the code can't deploy to a fresh org, it won't deploy to production.

## 5. Request Lifecycle & Governance Gates

Every interaction passes through three distinct "Gating Layers" to ensure performance and security. This diagram shows the journey of a single user request:

**Summary:** A 3-layer defense (Performance, Security, Governance). No request latency is measured, so no latency target is claimed. The measured numbers are the mobile LCP figures in [Technical Guide §2.11](./04-Technical-Guide.md#211-mobile-performance).

**Request lifecycle diagram**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'mainBkg': '#ffffff'}}}%%
    participant U as Visitor (LWR Site)
    participant B as Frontend Budget (LCP/JS)
    participant G as Security Gate (Guest Profile)
    participant A as Apex Governance (Governors)
    participant D as Data/Integration

    Note over U,B: Layer 1: Performance Budget
    U->>B: Request Page
    B->>B: Check Form Factor (Mobile?)
    alt is Mobile
        B-->>U: Serve the matrix, no graph engine
        Note right of U: no engine request
    else is Desktop
        B-->>U: Load D3_Library only when a graph view opens
        Note right of U: about 80 KB, on demand
    end

    Note over B,G: Layer 2: Zero Trust Security
    B->>G: Data Request (Apex or GraphQL)
    G->>G: Class access, object and field permissions (Portfolio_Guest)
    alt Not granted
        G-->>B: Request refused
    else Granted
        G->>A: Execute Logic
    end

    Note over G,A: Layer 3: Multitenant Governors
    A->>D: Read records, or a cache row a scheduled job wrote
    Note right of D: no callout while a visitor waits
    D-->>A: Payload
    A-->>B: Fixed response shape
    B-->>U: Render UI Update
```

**Permission checks:** a GraphQL read is checked against the guest's object and field permissions, and a field without them makes the query fail. An `@AuraEnabled` call needs class access in `Portfolio_Guest`. Inside Apex, the controllers that read records the guest cannot see (my Contact, experience highlights, the integration caches) do so in system mode through `without sharing` selectors with a fixed field list, and return only the shape the page needs.

**Limits:** nothing switches to a cached or deferred answer when a governor limit gets close. The protections that exist are a fixed number of queries per request, the caches that keep GitHub and Jira callouts out of page views, the rate limits in `RateWindowLimiter`, and the circuit breakers on Gemini, GitHub and Jira (`CircuitBreaker`).

## 6. The Three-Gate Approval Process

Each architectural decision is meant to pass three gates before it is built. They are a working checklist, not a workflow any tool enforces:

### Gate 1: Technical Feasibility

- Apex governor limits assessed (SOQL queries, DML rows).
- Related ADR documented (for example ADR-020: why the graph engine loads only when a graph view opens).

### Gate 2: Security & Privacy

- Guest User FLS matrix updated (SAS section 4.6 and `Portfolio_Guest`).
- Credentials rotated on the schedule in the [Maintenance Guide](./05-Maintenance-Guide.md#1-security-rotation-policy-cicd).

### Gate 3: Definition of Ready (DoR)

- User Story Acceptance Criteria defined in Jira.
- Mockups I have agreed before the build.

## 7. Business Impact of Executable Governance

These guardrails aren't just technical controls. They translate directly to business outcomes:

### Zero Runtime Costs

**Technical:** The portfolio demonstrates skills that reduce cloud spend in production environments.
**Business impact:** The same "No-VPC" and "Function URLs over API Gateway" patterns avoid the fixed monthly charges of a NAT Gateway and the paid API Gateway tier described in section 3. They are a design here, so no saving has been measured.

---

### Predictable Performance

**Technical:** Hard limits prevent runaway processes that cause outages.
**Business impact:** The 90% coverage gate and the full test run on every pull request stop a change that breaks a test before it reaches production. No count of prevented failures is kept, so none is claimed.

---

### Audit-Ready Architecture

**Technical:** Every API request is gated by OAuth and the rate limiter and written as one log line (`RequestUtil.logRequest`), and every evaluator token request writes an `API_Access_Request__c` record.
**Business impact:** The guest's access lives in one permission set in source (`Portfolio_Guest`), so a security review reads one file and its history.

---

### Fast Iteration

**Technical:** Quality gates catch issues in CI/CD, not in production.
**Business impact:** Delta deployments keep each release small, so features ship in small steps without giving up the gates above.

---

### Knowledge Transfer

**Technical:** The "Governor Rosetta Stone" table translates Salesforce-specific constraints into universal patterns.
**Business impact:** Bulkification, async processing, and lazy loading apply to any cloud platform (AWS, Azure, GCP). These patterns reduce database costs, improve response times, and increase system resilience across all architectures.

---

**Key Takeaway:** Governance isn't about saying "no". It's about architecting systems that succeed within real-world constraints while maintaining enterprise-grade quality, security, and observability. The free-tier constraints in this portfolio mirror the budget, security, and performance constraints of enterprise systems at scale.

Version: 1.0

Owner: Ryan Bumstead

Date: Live since October 2026

## 1. Integration Service Implementation

All external API calls originate from a secure **Named Credential** accessed via Apex, with no client-side access tokens used.

### 1.1 GitHub Integration (Live Feed)

- **Mechanism:** Uses the `GitHub_API` Named Credential, authenticated by the `GitHub_Auth` External Credential (a read-only token in the `GitHub_Principal` principal). Authenticated calls get 5,000 requests an hour.
- **Caching Strategy ([ADR-007](../adr/007-github-api-server-side-caching.md#amendment-2026-10-21-the-cache-objects-and-the-scheduled-refresh)):**
  - `IntegrationCacheRefreshScheduler` runs at :00, :15, :30 and :45 and enqueues `GitHubCacheRefreshJob` (`Queueable`, `Database.AllowsCallouts`, because scheduled Apex cannot call out synchronously).
  - The job reads the latest commits on `main` and inserts one row into the `Github_Cache__c` **custom object**, with the mapped commit list in `JSON_Payload__c`.
  - The same scheduled run also enqueues `SourceCacheRefreshJob` when a View source file is due, which fills `Source_Cache__c` from the GitHub contents API (section 2.14). It needs no schedule of its own.
  - Guests never call out. The `c-changelog` component reads the newest row through `DeliveryController.getRecentCommits(simulate)`.
- **Degraded Mode:**
  - A failed refresh inserts nothing, so the last good list keeps showing with its age.
  - Three consecutive failures open the `github` circuit breaker for 30 minutes, refreshes are skipped while it is open, and `DeliveryController` reports `DEGRADED`.
  - The cleanup batch keeps the newest row per cache object, so an outage never empties the page.
- **Logging.** When no `Portfolio_Config__mdt` record names a repository, and when a refresh fails, `GitHubCacheRefreshJob.refresh` writes one line through `PortfolioLog.info` (section 1.5) and returns without writing a cache row. The failure line names only the exception type, and the failure still counts toward the `github` breaker.

### 1.2 Jira Integration (Roadmap)

- **Authentication:** Basic Auth through the `Jira_API` Named Credential (`Jira_Auth` External Credential, `Jira_Principal` principal).
- **Refresh:** `JiraCacheRefreshJob`, enqueued by the same scheduler, runs the JQL `project = <key> AND labels = "portfolio-roadmap" ORDER BY updated DESC`, where the key is `Portfolio_Config__mdt.Jira_Project_Key__c` (`SPAP`), and inserts one `Jira_Cache__c` row from up to 100 issues. `JiraService.fetchRoadmap` posts to `/rest/api/3/search/jql`, follows `nextPageToken` and stops at `MAX_RESULTS` (100) issues, the last page or `MAX_PAGES` (5) requests, whichever comes first. Only issues labelled `portfolio-roadmap` become public (my decision, 2026-10-21).
- **Component:** `c-roadmap-viewer` reads the newest row through `DeliveryController.getRoadmap(simulate)` and places issues in To Do, In Progress and Done by Jira status category, so a renamed workflow status cannot empty a column. It never calls Jira. Cards name their epic as "Part of {name} | {key}" and epic cards come first in each column. Every column shows at most 8 cards (the `Roadmap_Column_Limit` setting, section 1.6, sent as `columnLimit`) with its own "Show all N" button and state, which keeps `aria-expanded` and the count in the column heading. Done shows its newest 8 by `updatedAt`, and To Do and In Progress keep the feed order and cut at 8. Earlier only Done was capped. I chose to cap every column, which replaced the test that pinned the Done only rule. A View source button in the roadmap header opens `roadmapViewer.js`, `roadmapViewer.html` and `DeliveryController.cls` (section 2.14).
- **Outage before and after.** While the feed's status is `SIMULATED`, `c-roadmap-viewer` and `c-changelog` each place `c-outage-compare` above their content (`showCompare`). It does not show for `DEGRADED`, a real open breaker. It is a static, labelled illustration, not a real error: a panel with no saved copy and no breaker, beside a three step trace of what the panel really does. Step one says no call was made to the source. Step two says the breaker counts a failed refresh and opens after the failure threshold in a row for the open minutes. Step three says the panel shows the last saved copy with its age, "N min ago", from the feed's `ageMinutes` or else `fetchedAt`. The two numbers come from the settings. `DeliveryController.getRoadmap` and `getChangelog` put `failureThreshold` and `openMinutes` on the feed, read from `CircuitBreaker.failureThreshold()` and `openMinutes()` (the `Circuit_Failure_Threshold` and `Circuit_Open_Minutes` settings, with the `CircuitBreaker` defaults of 3 and 30 when a record is missing). `c-roadmap-viewer` and `c-changelog` pass them to `c-outage-compare`, which holds no default of its own. When either is missing the step reads without that number ("After repeated failures in a row it opens") and the other part of the sentence stays, so changing a setting changes the text with no edit to the component ([ADR-022 amendments of 2026-10-29 and 2026-10-30](../adr/022-resilience-engineering-resilience-simulation-toggle.md#amendment-2026-10-29-the-before-and-after-for-the-outage-switch)).
- **Principal access:** the scheduling admin user reaches both principals through `Portfolio_Admin` (my decision, 2026-10-21). `Integration_Access` keeps them too, by my choice. `Portfolio_Guest` has neither.
- **Degraded Mode:**
  - After three consecutive failures, the `jira` circuit breaker skips Jira refreshes for 30 minutes, and `DeliveryController` reports `DEGRADED` while it is open.
  - With no usable cache row, the user sees a plain empty line ("Nothing on the roadmap yet"), and only a failed read shows "Roadmap temporarily unavailable".
- **Logging.** `JiraCacheRefreshJob.refresh` logs the same two cases (no config record, a failed refresh) through `PortfolioLog.info`, the failure by exception type only.

### 1.3 AI Content Generation (Agentforce on)

> [!NOTE]
> **Agentforce is built and its switch ships on** ([ADR-015 amendment of 2026-10-26](../adr/015-strategy-pattern-for-generative-ai.md#amendment-2026-10-26-agentforce-is-built-and-the-deferral-is-lifted)). `AgentforceService` runs a Prompt Builder template. The decision of 2026-10-02 to defer it is lifted.

- **One dispatch.** `ContentGenerationController.dispatch` tries Agentforce, then Gemini, then the Local Template (cover letters only), and records every attempt with its outcome (`served`, `skipped_off`, `skipped_open_circuit`, `failed`), its elapsed time and, on a failure, a short `detail` such as `HTTP 503` or the exception type, never a key or a URL with a query string. While the `gemini` or `agentforce` circuit breaker is open, that provider is skipped. Breaker state is written after every provider has been tried.
  - Agentforce is consulted only when `AgentforceService.isAvailable` is true: the `Agentforce` record of `AI_Provider_Config__mdt` has `Enabled__c` set, and the running user is not a site guest. The record ships with `Enabled__c` true, `Timeout_Ms__c` 20000, `Hourly_Budget__c` 120 and `Model_Or_Template__c` `Portfolio_Cover_Letter`. `AgentforceService.generateContent` runs that Prompt Builder template through `ConnectApi.EinsteinLLM.generateMessagesForPromptTemplate`, behind the `PromptTemplateClient` interface (the real client is `EinsteinPromptTemplateClient`, which names the application `PromptTemplateGenerationsInvocable`). The platform documents no test hook, so tests stand a stub in for the interface. The template has one input, `Input:Prompt`, which carries the whole prompt the dispatch built, and its content adds one line that holds the letter to the prompt's word range. Its model is `sfdc_ai__DefaultGPT41`. The call runs as the context user, who needs the Prompt Template User permission set. A Published template cannot be changed by a deploy, so a later wording change is a new version made in Prompt Builder.
  - Agentforce is held to `Hourly_Budget__c` calls per UTC hour (`AgentforceServiceBudget`), under the Developer Edition's 150 LLM generations an hour. The count is one `API_Rate_Window__c` row with the key `agentforce-hour|yyyyMMddHH`, read before the template runs and written with the breaker results after the last provider. Past the budget the attempt is `budget_exhausted` and the chain moves on. The read takes no lock, so calls in flight together can pass the budget by a few. A 429 or an answer from the limiter never counts as a breaker failure, and neither does a 401.
  - Measured in a scratch org on 2026-10-26 and 27, three cover letters called directly took 2.7 to 3.5 seconds and came back at 333 to 340 words. The first call through the API took 13.7 seconds, then 2.9 to 3.2 seconds. In production on 2026-10-27, after the deploy, one proof call served by Agentforce wrote a letter of 418 words, 10 seconds from page load to letter, over the 350 word cap. After the word limit line below, six letters in a row came back at 277 to 322 words in a scratch org loaded with production's grounding records (nine Agentforce calls in all, 2026-10-27). Production lengths after the deploy that carries that line are not measured yet.
  - Gemini is `gemini-2.5-flash`, the model on the `Gemini` record, through the Gemini API and the `Gemini_API` Named Credential, with a 60 second callout timeout from the same record (my decision 2026-10-21). `GeminiService.MODEL` (`gemma-4-31b-it`) is the code default, used only when the record names no model. Gemma 4 did not answer a full cover letter prompt inside the 60 seconds, so every letter fell back to the template, and Flash answered one in about 11 seconds in a scratch org. `GeminiService` reports a failure as text starting `Error: Unable to generate content.` or `Exception: `, which the dispatch treats as a failed attempt.
  - The Local Template serves a cover letter when Gemini fails. `LocalTemplateService` builds it in Apex from the records with no model: the company and role, the current title, the years on Salesforce, the current certifications and up to three ranked highlights or projects. It names no employer, holds no email or phone, never throws, and its last line says no model wrote it. Other content types answer 503 `ALL_PROVIDERS_UNAVAILABLE`.
- **Callers.** `PAPIAiGenerate.generate` (`POST /papi/ai/generate`) calls the dispatch for outside callers with a Bearer token and returns `provider`, `model`, `fallbackOccurred`, `latencyMs`, `attempts` and `promptShown`. The site's cover letter page (`coverLetterGenerator`) calls `ApiLabController.generateCoverLetter`. While the Agentforce switch is on and its breaker is closed, that method first posts to `POST /papi/ai/generate` with `provider` set to `Agentforce` through the `Portfolio_API` Named Credential, so the template runs as the integration user (a guest may not run generative AI). A 200 is the letter. Anything else runs the same dispatch **in process, as the site guest**, from Gemini on, then the template ([ADR-015 amendment on the in-process cover letter](../adr/015-strategy-pattern-for-generative-ai.md#amendment-2026-10-21-the-site-cover-letter-dispatches-in-process) and [the amendment of 2026-10-26](../adr/015-strategy-pattern-for-generative-ai.md#amendment-2026-10-26-agentforce-is-built-and-the-deferral-is-lifted)):
  - It checks `ApiLabController.AI_RATE_KEY` (`papi-ai:site-cover-letter`, 10 requests a minute, one bucket for every site visitor) with `ApiRequestContext.rateLimiter().checkKey` before the dispatch and writes the count with `ApiRequestContext.commitRateCounts()` after it. The key has the `papi-ai` prefix that `/papi/ai/` counts on, so the footer's "AI requests today" counts both paths. Over the limit, the page says "Too many cover letters were requested in the last minute. Try again in a minute."
  - It writes one log line through `PortfolioLog` with the path `aura:ApiLabController.generateCoverLetter`.
  - `Portfolio_Guest` holds the `Gemini_Auth-Gemini_Principal` principal for this. Agentforce is never consulted in process for a guest, only through the API call above.
  - The Agentforce call gets the `Agentforce` record's 20 second timeout, capped to what Gemini's timeout leaves of the 120 seconds Apex allows for callouts in a transaction, less a 2 second margin (`ApiLabController.CALLOUT_BUDGET_MS`). The attempt list shows the Agentforce attempt first.
  - The AI Lab shows my header over every letter, and the resume and the AI Lab share `c/profileLinks` for their links (LinkedIn, GitHub, Trailhead, Portfolio, Contact last). The footer's "AI requests today" counts a letter that went through the API once (`FooterController` takes off the `site-ai-proxied:cover-letter` marker the AI Lab adds when the API counted the letter).
  - Grounding as the guest goes through a `without sharing` selector that returns a fixed shape with no email, phone or owner field, because a guest sees only rows shared to it.
  - Why Gemini is not asked through the API: an earlier version of the page posted everything to the org's own `/papi/ai/generate` through the `Portfolio_API` Named Credential. A request that arrives as a callout from the same org may not call out again ("Callout loop not allowed"), so Gemini could never answer the page and every live letter came from the Local Template. A Connect API call did work inside such a request in a scratch org, so Agentforce takes the API route and Gemini stays in process.
- **Limits.** The Gemini key's free tier allowed Gemini 2.5 Flash 5 requests per minute and 20 requests per day when it was read from the AI Studio rate limit page on 2026-10-20 (Gemma 4 31B had 30 per minute, 16,000 tokens per minute and 14,400 per day). That is a recorded reading, not a live one. Once Google refuses a call, the template serves the cover letter.
- **Grounding.** `PortfolioGroundingService` adds featured projects and experience highlights to a cover letter prompt, ranked by keywords from the job title and description. It never selects Email, Phone or an owner field, strips anything shaped like an email address or phone number, and caps the JSON at 8,000 characters (about 2,000 tokens).
- **The cover letter prompt.** `ContentGenerationController.coverLetterPrompt(companyName, jobTitle, jobDescription)` is the one prompt builder, used by `generateCoverLetter` and by `ApiLabController.generateCoverLetter`. Its lines, in order: the instruction, then the word limit line (`coverLetterLengthLine`, built from `Cover_Letter_Min_Words` (250) and `Cover_Letter_Max_Words` (350)), the company, the role, the job description when given, the persona when the job points at one, and the grounding facts. Email and phone shapes are removed from the visitor's text first. The instruction is `Instruction__c` of the `AI_Prompt__mdt` record `Cover_Letter`, read with SOQL because `getInstance` returns only the first 255 characters of a long text field, and `COVER_LETTER_INSTRUCTION` in code is the fallback, so the wording can change without a code change. The letter is never cut. The word limit line reads "Word limit: 250 to 350 words, never more than 350.", says that limit overrides any later line about length, paragraphs or sentences, and fixes the shape: five paragraphs and no more, an opening of two sentences, three body paragraphs of three sentences each and a closing of two sentences, then the sign off, each sentence under 25 words. It does not start with "Length" on purpose. The Published template adds a sentence of its own for a `Length` line (write toward the upper number, in three body paragraphs of five sentences), and that sentence pushed letters past the maximum. A wording change in a Published template is a new version made in Prompt Builder, so the fix lives in the code line and the template is unchanged. `Ai_Max_Length` bounds only the `maxLength` a caller of `POST /papi/ai/generate` may ask for, and that endpoint builds its own prompt.
- **Persona.** `PortfolioGroundingService.inferPersona` reads Architect, Engineer, Consultant or Admin from the job title first and the description second, and the highlights tagged with that persona rank higher in the grounding. Admin stays an internal persona here and is not a focus a visitor can pick.
- **Generation config.** Every Gemini request sends a `generationConfig`: `maxOutputTokens` from `Ai_Max_Output_Tokens` (8192, because the model's reasoning counts against the limit and a limit hit while reasoning returns no letter) and `temperature` from `Ai_Temperature` (0.7).
- **Show your work.** The page shows the whole letter with its word count beside the provider badge. The badge shows the provider and model from the response. A panel the visitor opens shows the fallback flag, the round trip and generation time, the attempts (each with its `detail` when the dispatch reports one) and the prompt that was sent. The panel is built in Apex and the component, not by asking the model to reveal its prompt.
- **Fallback message.** When the template letter is used, the page says "The AI model could not be reached" if the Gemini attempt failed in under 1 second (`coverLetterGenerator.UNREACHABLE_MS`), and "The AI model was busy or too slow" otherwise. Each letter sends the GA4 event `ai_generation_completed`, and a request with no letter sends `ai_complete_failure`, both through the head script (section 2.8).
- **Footer.** `ContentGenerationController.providerStatus()` returns each provider's switch and state (`on`, `off`, `not built`) and `circuitOpenUntil` while its breaker is open, for the footer (section 2.6).
- **The Portfolio Guide Agent is in source and not live** ([ADR-036](../adr/036-portfolio-guide-agent.md)). It is a classic Bot (`Portfolio_Guide_Agent`, `EinsteinServiceAgent`) with a `GenAiPlannerBundle` on the ReAct planner and four topics: Career and Experience, Projects and Case Studies, Skills and Certifications, and Contacting Ryan, which has no action and points to the site's contact page. Three read only invocable actions serve the first three: `PortfolioAgentCareer`, `PortfolioAgentProjects` and `PortfolioAgentCredentials`. Each reads through `QueryDefinitions` in system mode (the five `PortfolioAgent*` records, section 1.7), returns JSON, and passes every text through `PortfolioAgentText.clean`, which removes email and phone shapes. No Contact is read and the client line is never read, so no email, phone or client name reaches the agent. No agent user is in source. The `Portfolio_Guide_Agent_Actions` permission set grants class access to the three actions and nothing else, for the agent's user.
  - The agent metadata needs API 65.0, so `sourceApiVersion` is 65.0.
  - It deploys to production inactive, at my word. No page embeds it and no Messaging channel is built.

### 1.4 System API Security (The "Twin" Pattern)

The APIs use platform-native OAuth 2.0 on both sides of the boundary ([ADR-027](../adr/027-platform-native-api-authentication.md)). The earlier design validated `client_id`/`client_secret` headers against Custom Metadata to simulate a MuleSoft policy point; that simulation was retired when MuleSoft left the architecture.

| Role         | Component                                              | Responsibility                                                          | Implementation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| :----------- | :----------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Provider** | External Client App (Client Credentials flow)          | **Authentication:** issues Bearer tokens; rejects bad callers upstream  | Runs as a dedicated integration user holding `Integration_Access` (read-only objects + execute on `SAPI*`/`PAPI*`). The platform rejects unauthenticated calls before Apex.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Consumer** | External Credential + `Portfolio_API` Named Credential | **Secure Storage:** holds the consumer key/secret in the platform vault | Used by `ApiLabController.invoke` (site proxy) and `PAPIHealth` (credential check). Token vending uses a second pair, `Portfolio_API_Token_Auth` and `Portfolio_API_Token`. No secret is ever stored in metadata or source.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Vendor**   | `PAPIAuthToken` (`POST /papi/auth/token`)              | **Evaluator access:** exchanges email + purpose for a short-lived token | The only REST class the guest user can execute ([ADR-028](../adr/028-evaluator-access-via-token-vending.md)). Shares `TokenExchangeService` with the proxy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Context**  | `ApiRequestContext` (shared by every REST class)       | **Contract hygiene:** headers, pagination, errors, cache, rate limits   | Reads `X-Request-Id` and `X-API-Version` (v1 when missing, v1 or v2 accepted, anything else 400, and sets `X-Request-Id` only when it generated one), adds the v1 deprecation headers, answers 410 after the sunset date (except on the token and health paths), bounds `limit` and `offset` (the offset to 2000), emits the `Error` schema with its `help` link, answers an unplanned exception with a fixed 500 that holds the correlation id (`serverError`), applies `Cache-Control` per resource, and enforces the [ADR-025](../adr/025-papi-fan-out-throttling-capacity-planning.md#amendment-2026-10-21) tiers through `RateWindowLimiter`. |

**API versions ([ADR-039](../adr/039-api-v2-and-the-v1-sunset.md)).** The URLs are the same for both versions and the header chooses the contract.

- **Selection.** `ApiRequestContext.version()` returns `v1` or `v2` and `isV2()` is the shortcut. A missing `X-API-Version` is v1. `v1` and `v2` are accepted in any letter case, so `V2` works, and anything else is a 400 that says to send v1 or v2. Every response carries `X-API-Version` in lower case with the version served and `Vary: X-API-Version`, which `appendHeader` adds to any value already set. The `Link` header is appended the same way. These checks and the sunset check run before the rate limiter, so a request they refuse spends none of the rate limit quota. Whether a given cache honours `Vary` is not yet checked.
- **v2 shape.** For the record endpoints, `SAPITransformer.toV2` shapes a body recursively. It drops `id`, each `xId` that has an `xKey` beside it, and `accomplishments`. `PAPITransformer.toV2` delegates to it. The token, health, AI generate, resume generate and portfolio config bodies are not shaped, because they are not lists of records (`UNSHAPED_PATHS`). v1 never calls it, so v1 bodies are unchanged.
- **v2 parameters.** `projectKey`, `experienceKey` and `certificationKey` take a public key only. A Salesforce Id gets 400 "<parameter> must be a public key, the key field of a record from GET <list route>. A Salesforce Id does not work in v2." and an old `*Id` name gets 400 "In v2 this filter is called projectKey, and it takes a public key. Rename projectId to projectKey." (`SAPIProjectSkill`, `SAPIProjectAsset`, `SAPIExperienceSkill`, `SAPIExperienceHighlight`, `SAPICertificationSkill`). The `/projects/{id}` path takes a key in v2 and answers 404 for anything else (`SAPIProject`). v1 keeps `projectId`, `experienceId` and `certificationId` and takes an Id or a key.
- **v1 headers.** Every v1 response carries `Link` with `rel="successor-version"` to `https://ryanbumstead.com/api-lab/reference?version=v2`, `Deprecation` (RFC 9745, `@` and unix seconds) once `Api_V1_Deprecation_Date` is set, and `Sunset` (RFC 8594, an HTTP date) once `Api_V1_Sunset_Date` is set, with `rel="deprecation"` and `rel="sunset"` entries in `Link` for those dates (`ApiRequestContext.addRetirementHeaders`). On an old `/v1/` URL the same method adds `Link` with `rel="canonical"` to the versionless URL and applies the path dates, and when both retirements apply it sends the earlier date of each pair ([ADR-040](../adr/040-versionless-api-urls.md)).
- **The 410.** From 00:00 UTC on the sunset date every v1 call except the three below, including one with no version header, gets 410 in the usual error envelope with `errorCode` `GONE` and a message that gives the retirement date and says to send `X-API-Version: v2`, with the v2 reference in `help` (`isGone`). v2 never returns it. The three exceptions are `POST /papi/auth/token`, `/sapi/health` and `/papi/health` (`SUNSET_EXEMPT_PATHS`). They keep their deprecation headers and are answered normally, so a client can still get a token and check that the API is up. Both settings are `Portfolio_Setting__mdt` records read as `yyyy-MM-dd` text, blank sends no header and never answers 410, and a value that is not a date reads as blank (section 1.6).
- **The path 410.** From 00:00 UTC on `Api_V1_Path_Sunset_Date` an old `/v1/` URL answers 410 `GONE` with a message that names the versionless path and never echoes a query value, whatever the version header says. The same three paths are exempt (`SUNSET_EXEMPT_PATHS`, now canonical paths, so both spellings of each). With the version also gone the message is the version sentence followed by the path sentence.
- **The site's own calls.** The Agentforce cover letter call (`ApiLabController`) and the `PAPIHealth` self call send `X-API-Version: v2`, so the sunset cannot reach them.

**Routing (ADR-040).** The URLs carry no version. `PAPIRouter` is mapped to `/papi/*` and `SAPIRouter` to `/sapi/*`, and each calls the static method of the existing handler for the route and verb, so a handler runs `ApiRequestContext.begin()` as before. The handler classes keep their `/v1/` `urlMapping`, and Apex REST picks the most specific mapping, so an old URL never reaches a router. `ApiRouting.routeParts` gives the route segments, and an old spelling gives none. An unknown route is `ApiRouting.notFound()` (404 in the error envelope), a verb a route lacks is `ApiRouting.methodNotAllowed` (405 in the same envelope with the usual headers and an `Allow` header), a caller with no token is `ApiRouting.unauthorized()` (401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`) and a token holder who asks the instance address for a token is `ApiRouting.forbidden()` (403). `ApiRequestContext.canonicalPath` drops the version segment, lower cases and trims, and `isLegacyPath` says which spelling came in. Class access is checked on the entry class only, so `PAPIRouter` keeps the old matrix itself: the guest reaches the token route and no other (401 elsewhere, on every PAPI route), and the integration user reaches every route but the token route (403 there). `SAPIRouter` is granted to the guest behind the same gate and answers it 401 on every SAPI route, so an anonymous caller is told how to get a token and not that a class is forbidden. `Portfolio_Guest` holds both routers and `Integration_Access` holds both routers. A new endpoint needs its handler and a row in the router. The `Api_Versionless_Urls` setting (`On` or `Off`, shipped `On`, anything but `Off` reads as `On`) switches the feature: Off, the routers answer 404 with the `/v1/` URL, old URLs stop being aliases (no `canonical` Link, no path dates, no path 410), and every Apex caller of our own API builds its URL with `ApiRoutes` (`papi`, `sapi`, `forCanonical`), which honours the switch. The API Lab reads it with the cacheable `ApiLabController.getVersionlessUrls`.

**Error messages (ADR-040, amendment of 2026-10-31).** Every sentence the API sends a person is a constant or a small builder in `ApiMessages`, so a test asserts the constant and not a copy of the text. A message says what happened, what the person needs and how to get it, in plain second person English with a closing period, and holds no exception type, no stack line and no class name (`ApiMessagesTest` checks the rules on every message). `errorCode` values do not change, and the `Error` object gains one field, `help`, a link to the code's entry on the API reference page with the spec of the API that was called (`ApiMessages.helpUrl`, for example `https://ryanbumstead.com/api-lab/reference?spec=papi&version=v2#error-bad-request`). The anchors are `error-` and the code in lower case with hyphens, one for each code in the Errors section of each v2 spec, and `c-api-reference` scrolls to the entry and focuses its heading (`errorEntry`).

- **An unplanned exception.** Every handler catches it with `ApiRequestContext.serverError`, which logs the exception type and the start of its message through `PortfolioLog` under the correlation id and answers 500 with a fixed message that holds the id. A failure while `begin()` applies the request rules, and any failure in either health check, takes the same road, so no exception type or stack line reaches a caller as the platform's `APEX_ERROR`. The rate count write in `ok` and `error` is bookkeeping and cannot turn an answer into an escaped exception.
- **The anonymous caller.** The 401 and the 403 are written by `ApiRequestContext.beginRefusal`, which applies no version rule, no `X-Request-Id` rule and no rate limit. A caller with no headers at all is told how to get a token, and spends none of the shared quota. The token URL in the message is the site's own address worked out at run time by `ApiSite.tokenUrl`: `Site.getBaseSecureUrl()` inside a site request, else the org's My Domain host with `.my.salesforce.com` replaced by `.my.site.com`, plus the site's path prefix, in the form `Api_Versionless_Urls` selects. It is never `ryanbumstead.com`, which redirects into the site, and a client that follows a redirect can turn the POST into a GET.
- **Retryable and `Retry-After`.** `retryable` is true only when the same request can succeed later with no change. A 503 that can recover and has no `Retry-After` gets 60 seconds from `error`, AI failures set their own (300 seconds, or the rest of the hour for the Agentforce budget), and the missing token credential is `retryable: false` with none. A lock timeout on the counter row is a 429 that says the API is busy (`RateDecision.busy`), apart from a used up limit.
- **Offset.** `offset` above 2000 is a 400, because the platform allows no larger SOQL offset (`ApiRequestContext.MAX_OFFSET`).
- **Persona.** `persona` matches in any letter case on every route and `/papi/resume/generate` echoes it as `Engineer`, `Architect`, `Consultant` or `Admin`. v1 and v2 share one reader. Both accept Engineer, Architect and Consultant, and both still accept `Developer`, which reads as Engineer, and `Admin`. The v2 specs list only the three focuses, and the v1 specs list those three plus Developer and Admin as aliases. Any other value is a 400.
- **The API Lab.** The Lab checks the email by the server's own pattern and checks the purpose before it sends. `ApiLabController` logs a callout failure and tells the visitor the Lab could not reach the API. A failed options read shows a line that says the filters can still be typed under Advanced.

**Plain text resume.** `GET /papi/resume/generate` honours `Accept: text/plain`. When the first media type in `Accept` is `text/plain` (`PAPIResume.wantsPlainText`, parameters after a semicolon ignored, the header name matched in any case), a 200 answer carries the generated text alone with `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8`. `PAPIResume.getResume` still runs `ApiRequestContext.ok` first, so the status, the rate count, the cache directive, the other headers and the request log line are the same as for JSON, and then replaces the body with the text. Any other `Accept` keeps the JSON body, and errors are always JSON. `scripts/api-smoke.sh` makes one such call and prints the first line.

**Rate limiting.** Rate limits are enforced in Apex by `RateWindowLimiter`, a custom-object counter: one `API_Rate_Window__c` row per caller key per minute. For SAPI and PAPI requests the caller key is `{tier}:{SHA-256 hex of the session id}`, or `{tier}:{user id}` when the session id is null. The token endpoint keys by `papi-token:{SHA-256 of lowercase email|source IP}`. Tiers: `sapi` 120, `papi` 15, `papi-ai` (`/papi/ai/*`) 10 requests per minute, over a fixed calendar minute. These are the shipped values of the `Api_Sapi_Rate_Per_Minute`, `Api_Papi_Rate_Per_Minute` and `Api_Ai_Rate_Per_Minute` settings (section 1.6). A request refused for an unsupported `X-API-Version` or a v1 410 is answered before the limiter runs and spends none of this quota. Request limit + 1 within a minute gets `429` `RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` with `Retry-After` set to the seconds left in the minute. The check (`RateWindowLimiter.checkKey`) reads and locks the row and writes nothing. The count is written with the response (`ApiRequestContext.ok`/`error`) or by `ApiRequestContext.commitRateCounts()` for non-REST callers, so resources may make callouts after `begin()`. Full rules: [ADR-025 amendment (2026-10-21)](../adr/025-papi-fan-out-throttling-capacity-planning.md#amendment-2026-10-21).

### 1.5 Logging (Nebula Logger, optional)

- **One seam.** `PortfolioLog.info(message)` writes a line to Nebula Logger when it is installed and to `System.debug` when it is not ([ADR-013 amendment on an optional install behind a seam](../adr/013-structured-logging-framework-nebula-logger.md#amendment-2026-10-21-an-optional-install-behind-a-seam)). It finds Nebula's `System.Callable` entry point, `CallableLogger`, at run time with `Type.forName` (namespace `Nebula` first, then none), so no source file depends on Nebula at compile time. CI and scratch orgs run without it.
- **One line per API request.** After the response is written, `ApiRequestContext` calls `RequestUtil.logRequest`, which writes `api request path=<path> status=<status> correlationId=<id> elapsedMs=<ms>`. The query string is cut off and no body, header value or token is logged. The site cover letter writes the same line with the path `aura:ApiLabController.generateCoverLetter`.
- **Never fails a request.** Nebula reports its own failures as `isSuccess` false, and the seam then falls back to `System.debug`. An exception inside the seam is caught.
- **Install (me, production only).** Nebula Logger's unlocked package with no namespace, installed by hand. Set log retention to 2 days in Nebula's settings, to stay inside Developer Edition storage. Entries carry the tag `portfolio`.

### 1.6 Operational Settings (`Portfolio_Setting__mdt`)

Operational values such as page sizes, rate limits, refresh intervals and display counts live in one custom metadata type, one record per value, so I can change one without editing code ([ADR-032](../adr/032-operational-settings-in-custom-metadata.md)).

- **The type.** `Portfolio_Setting__mdt`, visibility Public. `Number_Value__c` (Number 18,4) or `Text_Value__c` (Text 255) holds the value, `Min_Value__c` and `Max_Value__c` (Number 18,4) its safe range, and `Description__c` (Text Area 255) says in plain words what it controls and what range is safe. The label is the setting's plain name.
- **The accessor.** `PortfolioSettings` (`with sharing`) has `getInteger(developerName, fallback)`, `getDecimal(developerName, fallback)` and `getText(developerName, fallback)`. Every caller passes its own code constant as the fallback, so the code still says what the default is. A record that is missing, holds no value, or holds a number outside its `Min_Value__c` to `Max_Value__c` range gives the fallback, so a mistyped record never breaks a request. `getInteger` cuts a decimal to its whole part and gives the fallback for a number too large for an Integer. `getText` gives the fallback for a blank value and has no range.
- **One read per transaction.** The records are read once with `Portfolio_Setting__mdt.getAll()`, which runs no SOQL, and kept in a static map for the rest of the transaction.
- **Tests.** The test visible `PortfolioSettings.overrides` map sets a value without a record, and `overrideNumber(developerName, value)` is the short form. A key mapped to null reads as a missing record. `PortfolioSettingsTest` (16 tests) covers a shipped record, a missing one, a null value, both sides of the range and both bounds, no range, a number too large for an Integer, the overrides, one load per transaction with no SOQL, and a read as the site guest with no permission set assigned.
- **What stays in code.** Contract values (field lengths, enum and key strings, spec names) and layout constants (graph geometry, image sizes, label lengths) are not settings.
- **The records.** 37 ship in source (counted 2026-11-01). The first 23 shipped with the value the code used before, so the deploy that brought them changed no behaviour.
